section_summary: This section opens with U.S. Minister Roy T. Davis’s April 1933 report on an anti-Japanese press campaign in Panama, followed by newspaper articles, a cartoon, and memoranda alleging that Japanese barbers, fishermen, merchants, and ship representatives were conducting espionage, propaganda, and reconnaissance against the Panama Canal. It also contains criticism of those allegations, Julio Arjona’s account of Japanese activities dating from the First World War, a military attaché report concerning T. Tahara, and correspondence from J. Salvador Sánchez about supposed Japanese plans against the Philippines. The final pages consist largely of file-transfer and charge sheets, followed by a December 1934 despatch and the beginning of a memorandum about an anonymous threat to explode Gatun.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1504: Japanese in Panama
subfiles.from: Roy T. Davis, United States Legation, Panama
subfiles.about: Reports Nelson Rounsevell’s newspaper campaign alleging Japanese espionage and a potential sabotage threat to the Panama Canal.
subfiles.summary: Davis reports that The Panama American began an anti-Japanese campaign on April 21, claiming that Japanese fishermen, barbers, shirt makers, merchants, and restaurateurs were spies rather than genuine workers. He compares Rounsevell’s estimates with a Canal police census listing 171 adult Japanese men in Panama City and Colón. The despatch also recounts an unverified speech attributed to Amaro and transmits newspaper clippings and Julio Arjona’s memorandum.

subfiles.title: Rambling, Gambling and Publishing: Japanese Espionage on the Isthmus
subfiles.about: Claims that Japanese shops and fishing boats in Panama conceal a large espionage organization capable of attacking the Canal.
subfiles.summary: Rounsevell contrasts British protection of its citizens with the expected American response to two soldiers arrested in China. He alleges that Japanese have photographed Canal Zone defenses for years and that unprofitable barber shops, shirt factories, and fishing boats are espionage covers. He condemns U.S. military and naval intelligence for allegedly allowing a Japanese organization large enough to sabotage the Canal.

subfiles.title: Existe en Panamá sistema de espionaje del Japón
subfiles.about: Spanish version of Rounsevell’s article alleging an extensive Japanese spy system on the Isthmus.
subfiles.summary: The article repeats allegations that Japanese barbers, shirt makers, and fishermen are actually trained naval or military agents. It describes supposed photography near Corozal and Fort Clayton and claims the Japanese community could destroy the Canal within an hour. It closes by accusing authorities at Quarry Heights and American intelligence services of ignoring the danger.

subfiles.title: What Are 70 Japanese Shops Doing in Panama?
subfiles.about: Questions how approximately seventy Japanese barber shops and 280 barbers can remain solvent despite little visible trade.
subfiles.summary: Lung claims Japanese barber shops evade municipal taxes, employ more barbers than their business could support, and may be subsidized by Japan or engaged in covert activities. He identifies shops in Calidonia and on North and Central Avenues and notes that one barber owned a racehorse at Juan Franco. The article urges Panamanian police to watch the shops, including in connection with narcotics investigations.

subfiles.title: Las barberías japonesas están alineadas en forma igual a la de tanques de guerra
subfiles.about: Spanish version of Lung’s report portraying Japanese barber shops as suspicious, unprofitable, and possibly subsidized.
subfiles.summary: The article says approximately seventy Japanese barber shops operate at strategic points in Panama City without paying municipal taxes. It compares the establishments to tanks prepared for an offensive and suggests their occupants read about espionage and world conquest while receiving few customers. Specific shops in Calidonia and on North Avenue are cited.

subfiles.title: Better Open Your Eyes, Uncle!
subfiles.about: Editorial cartoon warning Uncle Sam to recognize an alleged Japanese threat.
subfiles.summary: The page reproduces a cartoon titled “Better Open Your Eyes, Uncle!” as an enclosure to despatch No. 1504. Its placement identifies it as part of The Panama American’s campaign urging greater vigilance against alleged Japanese espionage in Panama.

subfiles.title: Ninguna barbería de Panamá paga impuestos al municipio
subfiles.about: Clarifies that no barber shops in Panama, regardless of nationality, were then paying the disputed municipal tax.
subfiles.summary: El Tiempo states that Japanese establishments were not uniquely evading the barber-shop tax. All barbers had stopped paying after claiming professional status when the municipal council attempted to raise the levy. The question remained before the provincial governor.

subfiles.title: Nelson Rounsevell y el espionaje japonés
subfiles.about: Denounces Rounsevell’s and Lung’s espionage accusations as sensationalism and an affront to Panamanian sovereignty.
subfiles.summary: The writer argues that The Panama American serves U.S. interests and has presented no proof that Panama’s Japanese residents are spies. The letter compares the campaign with an earlier newspaper controversy involving Eliot Alves and the El Remance mines and recalls Rounsevell’s expulsion from Chile. It urges the Panamanian government to reject pressure to police Japanese residents merely as a guardian of U.S. interests.

subfiles.title: Rambling, Gambling and Publishing: Amaro’s Waterfront Speech
subfiles.about: Alleges that Catalino Amaro delivered anti-American Japanese propaganda at the Panama waterfront and criticizes U.S. military administration.
subfiles.summary: Rounsevell says Amaro displayed supposed official cables, falsely reported the sinking of two American cruisers, and justified Japanese operations in Manchuria as protection against the United States. He portrays the speech as one instance of a broad Japanese propaganda campaign. The second page attacks General Brown and military governance for neglecting defense while interfering in civilian affairs and generating anti-American resentment.

subfiles.title: Jap Merchants in Panama Ignore 75 Per Cent Law and Undersell Local Owners
subfiles.about: Accuses Japanese retailers of violating Panama’s 75-percent local-labor law and using subsidized prices to conceal other activities.
subfiles.summary: Lung names several Central Avenue and I Street businesses alleged to employ too few or no Panamanians. He claims Japanese stores sell goods below normal prices despite apparent losses and suggests outside financial support. The article also invites investigation of the shops in relation to narcotics trafficking.

subfiles.title: Rambling, Gambling and Publishing: Registration, Taxation, and Espionage
subfiles.about: Calls for surveillance of Japanese residents and investigations into their registration, taxes, labor practices, and alleged espionage.
subfiles.summary: Rounsevell alleges that Japanese residents receive favored treatment while avoiding registration, taxation, and labor regulations. He presents registration and occupational figures and urges Americans to report suspicious Japanese activity to military, naval, police, and diplomatic authorities. He argues that barber shops facilitate intelligence gathering and that fishing boats provide access to Canal defenses in Panama Bay.

subfiles.title: Rambling, Gambling & Publishing: Spanish Version
subfiles.about: Spanish version of Rounsevell’s call to investigate and monitor Japanese residents in Panama.
subfiles.summary: The article repeats claims that Japanese residents enjoy favored-nation privileges while contributing little to Panama and evading registration and taxes. It identifies fishing and barbering as occupations useful for espionage and claims Japanese fishing boats threaten Canal defenses. It also questions enforcement of import duties, sign taxes, salary taxes, and the 75-percent Panamanian labor requirement.

subfiles.title: 74 Japanese Fishermen Roam Waters of Panama Bay During Entire Night
subfiles.about: Alleges that Japanese fishermen use night fishing as cover for hydrographic reconnaissance near Canal fortifications.
subfiles.summary: Lung describes seventy-four Japanese fishermen, their Panama City residences, boats, and nightly movements in Panama Bay. He accuses them of using dynamite, unfairly competing with Panamanian fishermen, and sounding coastal waters for military purposes. Their concentration on the Pacific side is presented as evidence of Japanese ambitions in the Pacific.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for the Minister of the United States of America
subfiles.about: Presents Arjona’s observations and suspicions concerning the growth and activities of Panama’s Japanese community.
subfiles.summary: Arjona recounts cooperating with U.S. Army and Canal Zone police officers in surveillance of German and Japanese communities during the First World War. He alleges that many Japanese barbers are army officers, fishermen have charted Panama Bay and the Gulf of Panama, and retailers are employees of the Japanese government. He recommends discreet surveillance and stronger measures to protect the Canal, while also criticizing Panamanian communism and anti-American politicians.

subfiles.title: Translation of Julio Arjona’s Memorandum
subfiles.about: English translation of Arjona’s Spanish memorandum on alleged Japanese military, commercial, and hydrographic activities.
subfiles.summary: The translation describes Arjona’s wartime surveillance work with American Army and Canal Zone police personnel. It repeats his belief that Japanese barbers were army officers, fishermen had obtained soundings of Panama Bay and the Gulf, and government-backed retailers were concentrating in the Canal’s terminal cities. Arjona urges confidential preventive action by both Panama and the United States.

subfiles.title: Japanese Spy Campaign by Panama American
subfiles.from: Office of the Military Attaché, American Legation, Panama; Alex A. Cohen
subfiles.about: Forwards an editorial accusing T. Tahara of directing Japanese espionage on the Isthmus.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum quotes a May 17 Rounsevell editorial claiming that T. Tahara posed as a steamship representative while serving as a Japanese naval intelligence officer. Tahara is alleged to have outranked Vice Admiral Hyakutake, arranged activities during the visit of the cruisers Iwate and Yakumo, and directed agents concealed as barbers, fishermen, and shirt makers. The editorial also alleges that information passed through a German employee of Boyd Brothers in Cristóbal to Tahara’s files at Hotel Washington.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Conversation with Mr. Taketomi
subfiles.about: Cross-references a memorandum about discussing American press reports of Japanese spies in Panama with a Japanese Embassy counselor.
subfiles.summary: The file note directs researchers to file 711.94/831. The referenced memorandum records a conversation with Mr. Taketomi, counselor of the Japanese Embassy, concerning American newspaper stories about Japanese spies in Panama.

subfiles.title: Letter Concerning Japanese Plans and Activities
subfiles.about: Reports secondhand claims about Japanese naval and Philippine plans and also offers a disinfectant product for government purchase.
subfiles.summary: Sánchez says earlier reports of a Japanese plan against the Philippines were confirmed and recounts an Italian salesman’s conversations with an influential Japanese butler in Panama. He alleges that Japan intended to expand its fleet through contracts with foreign countries and cites a supposed shipbuilding agreement with Brazil. The letter then shifts to promoting a deodorizing disinfectant for hospitals, military facilities, government offices, and other institutions.

subfiles.title: Translation of Sánchez’s Letter
subfiles.about: English translation of Sánchez’s letter concerning alleged Japanese plans and his disinfectant business proposal.
subfiles.summary: The translation recounts claims that a timely fleet movement frustrated a Japanese plan against the Philippines. It reports hearsay from an Italian traveler about a Japanese servant in Panama who predicted war with the United States and discussed Japanese shipbuilding schemes. Sánchez also suggests gathering intelligence in Brazil and Peru before offering his disinfectant formula or product to the U.S. government.

subfiles.title: Translator Routing Slip
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Communications and Records
subfiles.about: Records that the original document was sent for translation of its enclosure.
subfiles.summary: This administrative sheet notes receipt on March 2, 1934. It states that the original was forwarded to the translator so that the enclosure could be translated.

subfiles.title: Despatch Transmitting a Letter Concerning Japanese Activities
subfiles.from: Fred Morris Dearing, American Embassy, Lima
subfiles.about: Transmits Sánchez’s January 8 letter while judging its information to be of little value.
subfiles.summary: Dearing identifies Sánchez as a former resident of northern Peru who had previously supplied similar reports. He states that the new letter does not appear very valuable but forwards it for Department files and possible use by the legation in Panama. The two pages are duplicate impressions of the same despatch.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Spanish Copy of Sánchez’s Letter
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy of Sánchez’s report on alleged Japanese plans and his proposal to sell a disinfectant.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats the allegations that Japanese plans against the Philippines had been delayed and that Japan sought to increase its fleet through foreign shipbuilding contracts. It again cites information attributed to an Italian traveler and a Japanese servant in Panama. The concluding portion offers samples, the product, or the formula for a disinfectant.

subfiles.title: Charge Slip for File 894.20219
subfiles.about: Records an internal charge or temporary removal of file 894.20219.
subfiles.summary: The form is headed “Charge Slip” and identifies file 894.20219. Much of the charge information is illegible, but it appears to bear the date October 25, 1934, and a reference to a memorandum.

subfiles.title: Faint Copy of Despatch No. 546: Japanese Activities
subfiles.from: Antonio C. Gonzalez, American Legation, Panama
subfiles.about: Transmits an office memorandum dated December 29, 1934, concerning Japanese activities.
subfiles.summary: This badly faded copy records the transmission of a memorandum on Japanese activities. A handwritten Department notation asks whether Military Intelligence could be excused from receiving the material because it already had the information in Panama.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 546: Japanese Activities
subfiles.from: Antonio C. Gonzalez, American Legation, Panama
subfiles.about: Forwards an office memorandum concerning Japanese activities in Panama.
subfiles.summary: Gonzalez encloses an office memorandum dated December 29, 1934. The despatch provides no substantive detail beyond identifying the subject as Japanese activities and transmitting the enclosure to Washington.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Anonymous Threat to Explode Gatun
subfiles.to: Department of State, as enclosure to despatch No. 546
subfiles.about: Begins an account of an anonymous note threatening to demonstrate Japanese superiority by exploding Gatun.
subfiles.summary: James Ryan informed the legation that he had received a carbon copy of a note reading, “Fools defy Nippon. We prove superior exploding Gatun. Signed BANZAI.” The author notified Admiral Crosley, General Fiske, Colonel Ridley, and Captain Ketcham, and later received an apparently identical note addressed to the American Minister. Vice Consul Warner was asked to interview Detective Myers; the memorandum continues beyond this section.
